questions.statement: The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor.
questions.context: A defining relative clause, where the pronoun acts as the subject.

options.feedback: Correct! Who is the subject of lives, and a defining clause needs a subject to complete the sentence.
Which refers to things, and the woman is a person.
Whose expresses possession, and there is no possession in this sentence.
Whom is the object form and would need a verb after it, but lives is already complete.

questions.explanation:
A defining relative clause is essential to the meaning of the noun. It needs its own subject and verb, which is who in this sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The student ___ essay won the prize comes from León.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a possessive pronoun.

options.feedback: Correct! Whose shows possession of the essay, and the relative pronoun refers back to the student.
Who would be the subject of the clause, but the clause has no verb of its own here.
Which cannot be used for people, and the student is a person.
What cannot be used with an antecedent noun, and there is a clear antecedent here.

questions.explanation:
Whose expresses possession and works with a noun directly after it. The noun it modifies is the possessive object, and the clause has no separate verb of its own.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The film ___ we watched last night was excellent.
questions.context: A defining relative clause where the pronoun is the object.

options.feedback: Correct! That is the neutral object pronoun and works for both people and things.
Which would also be possible in formal English, but that is the safer general choice for an object.
What has no antecedent, and this clause clearly refers back to the film.
Where asks about a place and cannot stand in for the object of watched.

questions.explanation:
That is the most versatile relative pronoun. It can be a subject or an object and it works with both people and things, which is why it is the default in exam answers.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The teacher ___ we spoke to was very patient.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a preposition at the end.

options.feedback: Correct! The relative pronoun is the object of the preposition to, and that is the neutral choice here.
In English the preposition stays at the end of the clause, and to who is not a possible order.
Which would restrict the verb to things, and the teacher is a person.
What cannot stand for an object that already has an antecedent.

questions.explanation:
After a preposition the relative pronoun becomes the object of that preposition. The preposition itself is left at the end of the clause in formal English.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The house ___ we grew up in has been sold.
questions.context: A defining relative clause introduced by a prepositional phrase.

options.feedback: Correct! In a prepositional phrase the relative adverb replaces the pronoun and the preposition disappears.
In which is possible in formal English, but where is shorter and the standard everyday choice.
That would need the preposition as well, and the sentence already omits it in favour of where.
What cannot be used with an antecedent noun, and the house is a clear antecedent.

questions.explanation:
Where, when and why replace the pronoun plus preposition combination. We grew up in it becomes where we grew up.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: That is the year ___ the school opened.
questions.context: A defining relative clause about time.

options.feedback: Correct! When replaces the preposition in a time phrase and acts as the subject of opened.
In which is longer and less natural, and when is the standard relative adverb for time.
Which would need the preposition at the end, such as which the school opened in, which is clumsy here.
That can be a subject pronoun but it cannot replace a time preposition on its own.

questions.explanation:
Relative adverbs replace the pronoun plus the preposition: in which becomes when, in which became when. The clause then has its own subject and verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She is the only student ___ passed the exam.
questions.context: A defining relative clause about a reason.

options.feedback: Correct! The relative pronoun is the subject of passed, so who is the natural choice.
That would also be grammatically possible, but who is more precise when the pronoun is the subject of a clause about a person.
Which refers to things, and the student is a person.
Why expresses a reason, and this clause gives no reason.

questions.explanation:
When the relative pronoun is the subject of the clause, the clause has a full verb of its own. Who and which both work as subjects, and the choice depends on the antecedent.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He is the man ___ car I repaired last week.
questions.context: A defining relative clause joined to another relative pronoun.

options.feedback: Correct! Whose links the clause to the noun car and expresses possession.
Who would need a verb after it, and the clause has repaired with no further subject.
Which would refer to the man rather than the car, and it cannot express possession.
That would be the subject of the clause, and the possessive link would be lost.

questions.explanation:
A defining clause can hold two different relationships at once. Whose connects the man to the car as its possessor, while I is the subject of repaired.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The project ___ I was working on is finally finished.
questions.context: A defining relative clause where the pronoun is the object of a preposition.

options.feedback: Correct! The pronoun is the object of on, and that is the neutral object form.
Putting the preposition before the pronoun is only acceptable in very formal English and is not the everyday form.
What has no antecedent and cannot be used with a preceding noun.
Which would restrict the verb to things, and the project is a project but the safer form is that.

questions.explanation:
The preposition can sit in two places. In everyday English it closes the clause, while in formal English it is placed before the relative pronoun.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The man ___ was talking to my brother is the new head of the department.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a past continuous verb.

options.feedback: Correct! The clause needs a subject before the past continuous, and who supplies it.
A bare auxiliary would leave the clause without a subject of its own.
Which refers to things, and the man is a person.
Whose expresses possession, and there is nothing possessed in this clause.

questions.explanation:
A defining relative clause can hold any tense, including continuous forms. The only requirement is that the clause has its own subject and verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The city ___ I was born has changed enormously.
questions.context: A defining relative clause about a place, formal version.

options.feedback: Correct! The preposition plus relative pronoun is the formal alternative to where.
In that introduces a result or a fact rather than a place, and the clause has no verb.
At would suggest a point rather than a location, and the standard preposition for a place is in.
What cannot follow a preposition with a noun antecedent, so this combination is not possible.

questions.explanation:
Where and in which mean the same thing. Where is shorter and more common, while in which is the form that formal and academic writing often prefers.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The book ___ you recommended was out of print.
questions.context: A defining relative clause where that is the object.

options.feedback: Correct! That is the object of recommended and works for both people and things.
Which is also valid in formal English, but that is the safer general choice with an object pronoun.
What would carry the meaning inside itself and cannot stand after a noun antecedent.
Where replaces a place preposition, and recommended has no place here.

questions.explanation:
That covers both the subject and the object positions. That you recommended is the object, and that which changed the country is the subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Cortazar, ___ wrote Rayuela, was an Argentine writer.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a proper noun as the antecedent.

options.feedback: Correct! Who is the subject of wrote and refers to a person.
Which would refer to a thing, and the antecedent is a person.
That would also be possible, but who is more precise with a person subject in formal writing.
Whose would claim that Cortazar possesses the novel, which is not the relationship in this sentence.

questions.explanation:
Relative pronouns are chosen by function, not just by the type of antecedent. The subject role with a person calls for who, and the verb wrote confirms that role.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The students ___ failed will retake the exam in March.
questions.context: A defining relative clause attached to a plural antecedent.

options.feedback: Correct! The pronoun is the subject of failed and the verb already shows a plural subject, so who is correct.
Which would be wrong here because failed is a finite verb and the clause needs a person subject.
What cannot be used with an antecedent noun, however plural it is.
Whose expresses possession and there is nothing possessed in this clause.

questions.explanation:
The finite verb of the relative clause tells you whether the pronoun is a subject or an object. A finite verb needs a subject, and that is who or which.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This is the only option ___ works on every phone.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a that-clause, where the pronoun is the subject.

options.feedback: Correct! That is the subject of works, and it is the standard choice for things in this position.
Which is possible in formal English, but that is the everyday form when the pronoun is the subject of a clause about a thing.
What cannot be preceded by a noun antecedent, and the option is a clear antecedent.
Where replaces a place preposition, and works on every phone has no place element.

questions.explanation:
With a subject pronoun for a thing, both that and which work, and that is the more common choice. What is never allowed with an antecedent.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The people ___ we spoke to at the party were from Canada.
questions.context: A defining relative clause in a sentence with a preposition at the end.

options.feedback: Correct! The formal object pronoun is the correct form after a preposition at the end of the clause.
Who would leave the clause without an object, because spoke needs one before to.
That is the object form, but the formal register of the question points to whom being the better answer.
Which cannot refer to people, and the people here is the antecedent.

questions.explanation:
Whom is the formal object form of who. It appears mainly after a preposition at the end of a relative clause, and the everyday alternative is that.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: That is the reason ___ she left the company.
questions.context: A defining relative clause about a thing, with a relative adverb for reason.

options.feedback: Correct! Why replaces for which and expresses the reason in the clause.
For which is the formal equivalent but reads awkwardly, and why is the standard relative adverb.
That could be a subject pronoun, but the clause has no verb of its own to be the subject of.
Which cannot replace the preposition for on its own without leaving the sentence incomplete.

questions.explanation:
Why, where, when and how replace their pronoun plus preposition equivalents. The reason why is the usual phrase in everyday English.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which is the film ___ won the award last year?
questions.context: A defining relative clause in a question form.

options.feedback: Correct! That is the subject of won, and the wh question in the main clause is unrelated to the relative pronoun.
Which is valid in formal English, but that is the more common subject pronoun in a question of this kind.
What cannot be used with the noun film, which is already a clear antecedent.
When replaces a time preposition, and there is no time phrase in the clause.

questions.explanation:
A wh question in the main clause does not affect the relative pronoun inside the clause. The two structures work independently, and which film is answered by the film itself.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The film ___ directed by that woman won three awards.
questions.context: A defining relative clause with a reduced form.

options.feedback: Correct! A defining clause can be reduced by dropping the pronoun and the auxiliary when the pronoun is the subject.
A reduced relative clause drops the relative pronoun and keeps the verb, so a finite verb is not part of the reduced form.
A present participle would be a reduced form of an active clause in progress, and the film is not directing.
A past perfect is not part of a reduced defining clause, and the verb has no auxiliary to attach it to.

questions.explanation:
A relative clause whose pronoun is the subject can be reduced: the film that was directed becomes the film directed. The meaning stays the same and the clause becomes an adjective phrase.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The students ___ sit in the front row are preparing a show.
questions.context: A defining relative clause where the pronoun is the subject and the verb is passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The clause needs a subject for the finite verb sit, and who supplies it.
Which would restrict the verb to things, and the students are people.
That is also valid, but who is the more precise subject pronoun for a person.
A bare verb would leave the clause with no subject, because the relative pronoun occupies that position.

questions.explanation: A finite verb inside a relative clause always needs a subject, and that subject is the relative pronoun. Omitting it would leave the clause incomplete.
questions.subject: ingles
